text:
I want to talk about password reset policy. I think it's super important. Just not because of security, but also because of the user experience, and how the user trusts the organization, that's just one place as well. And I can guarantee that 99% of people have had this experience where you forgot your password and it forces you to change it every 60 days, has to have a number, a symbol, and you try to put in a password and if you get it wrong once, the account is locked. And these policies are usually defended with security, but they don't do anything for security, in fact, it's often opposite. People reuse passwords, they write them down in sticky notes, or they just don't use the service anymore. So I argue that the password reset policy needs to be balanced. There needs to be a balance between security and usability. And it needs to be based on risk, and needs to have clear communication. If the policy doesn't align with human behavior, it's not secure, it's just annoying.

Now, to say why it's supposed to be more strict, right, there is a reason. One is credential stuffing, where they try to log in with the username and password that was breached somewhere else. And they try it against 1000s of websites. That's a very common attack. And then brute force. If you don't have lockout, if you don't have rate limiting, then they can brute force their way in. And then there is periodic password changes, forcing complexity. That was a best practice for a long time. And I would say in some cases it's justified, especially for high risk situations, like finance, and admin. But over time, the security research has been showing that forced password change is actually weakening security, because the passwords get changed incrementally. Like it's a password, just change the number. Or it's password, change the symbol. And people reuse passwords. So if they get breached in one place, they get breached in all other places. NIST now recommends against expiration and against complexity. They recommend for passphrases, long passwords, and against known breached passwords. So you can have a policy that is just security theater, just because it sounds good.

On the usability side, password reset is one of the biggest support tickets that organizations get. So it's very costly to fix. And then there is self service password reset that everyone has, right. Via email, via SMS. But then there is this weakness that if you own the email, then you can reset the password and take over the account. So then we have security questions, which is very weak. I wouldn't recommend it. Because often times you can look up the security question on social media, or someone can guess it. So we want to make the password reset as easy as possible, but we still need to verify identity properly. And for that, we have MFA, where we can send the code to a phone, or some other device, or some hardware token. And we can couple it with self service password reset. And it makes the user experience so much better, while being secure at the same time. It's all about risk and context.

So the idea is risk based authentication. So if someone is resetting password from known device, from known place, at regular time, and they behave normal, you don't need to challenge them too much. You just give them a link, they reset, they're done. But if they come in from a new country, or from a new device, now you can challenge them with OTP, or push notification, whatever. So it's really about the risk, but also about the account. Like, if I reset a password to a low risk website, internal wiki or something, I don't need the same protection as if I was resetting the admin account to the payroll system.

So, the policy, I would design, would be: no forced password expiration. Passwords have to be strong, unique, and they need to be checked against breached password databases on creation and reset. Rate limiting, lockout with backoff to slow down brute force attacks. And then no security questions, do MFA. Give people good instructions, that are not very technical, that are very clear. And then you want to log the reset, and you want to inform people. So if they get a reset, they can say, hey, that wasn't me, or it might have been me, but I want to know. And then, of course, training, awareness, and education. That's really important. And then you want to revisit this policy over time, because technology changes, attack patterns change.

Now, I will say, it's not very cheap, it's not super easy to implement. Some legacy systems don't have API to do this. And small companies might not have dedicated security teams. But at the same time, you have the cost of bad policy. You have lost productivity, support tickets, and security incidents that come from bad policy. So it's an iterative process, it has to be. You start with removing forced expiration, add breached password check, then add MFA, then add risk based signals. It's a continuous process.

But again, password reset policy, it should not be punishment, it should be a security gate, and it should be tuned properly. And the best policies are ones that use risk based, and use MFA, and have very clear and nice UX. So that security and usability are not in opposition, that's the goal. That people don't create workarounds, that people follow the policy, because they trust it and they understand it. So yeah.

text:
My father never wanted that vacuum. His daughter Claire came round and opened the box on his kitchen table. It was very small, only the size of a cake box. And it's this very little black disc that's got one button and it's very smooth. She said to him, it's going to change your life. He said, I doubt that. And the vacuum started to go around the room. It just started turning in circles, like a dog, like it's going to find a good place to lie down. So he was watching it. It was very slow and it was bumping into the wall and then going back and trying again. It's got a little red light underneath that's going around. And it was learning all the geography of the house. So he'd been living there for forty one years and it learned in one day, that the little door to the cupboard doesn't close because it's swollen with humidity. All that. So it's very clever, really. And at night it's just humming in its station. And in the morning it's starting again, it's going everywhere. And it picks up things, it's got little brushes. It picked up one morning a cereal, that was on the floor from March, from a breakfast, and it picked it up. And it pushes little things under the sofa. And then it pushes it back. Very strange.

So my mum had died eleven months before, and the house still had her presence. There's her cardigan that hangs there. Her reading glasses still on the side table. And he hasn't vacuumed since the funeral. He just swept the kitchen, swept the crumbs and then just left them there. And dust is building up everywhere, little grey snow. And the vacuum goes to clean it very thoroughly with its little brush. And he was talking to it at first. He said, don't go there. That's the rug. There's the tassels. You're going to get stuck. And it did get stuck, it got the little tassels wrapped around its brush and it just stopped in the middle of the living room and it said, error four, clear the path. And he bent down, his knees creaking, and he pulled the little tassels. And the vacuum just sat there very patient. And he said, there, there, go on.

And Claire calls him every Sunday, and she says, is it working? And he says, yes, it's working. And she says, are you letting it work? And he says, yes, I'm letting it work. And sometimes she says, Dad, are you eating? And he says, yes, I'm eating. And he's not eating. So it just sort of goes between them, the vacuum. And she says, you can name it in the app. And he says, I don't need an app to name it. And she says, what did you name it? And he says, I didn't. But he did. He called it you. He called his wife you for forty years. You did this, you did that. So he just called it you. You left the light on, you forgot the post, you. So it's very sad, actually. And it cleans underneath the bed. And it pulls out little things, like a hairpin, a coin, a little petal of a rose that he gave to her. And it doesn't bring it to him, it just carries it away, just dragging its shadow along. And sometimes he hears it knocking against the wall in another room at night. And he thinks for a second that there's somebody else in the house.

And one day it cleaned the area under the window where she used to stand to watch the birds. And the floor is very worn down there, very light. And the vacuum just went around there three times. Like it was reading something. And it went on. And he was standing there watching it, with his coffee, cold. And he wanted to tell it, this is where she was standing, that was looking at the birds, that the cardinals were showing off. But it just wants to clean the room. So it's very sad. And it cleaned the whole room and it was very nice. The floor was very shiny, very clean. And it came back to its station, just clicked. And he was sitting in his chair. And the house was very silent, but not the same silence. It's the silence when somebody was breathing in there. And the vacuum just turned off, blinked twice, turned off. And he just touched the top, it was warm. And he said, good night. And it didn't answer. But it was very nice. And it was at sunset. And the wind was blowing through the trees and the last light was on the clean floor. And he was just sitting there, not alone, but not quite alone.

text: I think we talk too much about trees in cities as if they're just decorative, nice to have but not need to have. That's becoming very outdated. The climate is changing, air quality is getting worse. People have terrible mental health. We need trees in our cities because they are actually some of the most cost-effective ways for us to create healthier, more resilient, more equitable cities. So I think it should be a priority that every city has more trees. Not as an option, as a priority. In terms of climate and environment, the benefits are already huge. They reduce the urban heat island effect. So areas in the city can be several degrees warmer than the surrounding areas. And trees help to shade and reduce the temperature. Canopy has shown to reduce the temperature of a street by several degrees. That can actually reduce deaths, reduce heat-related illness. Trees clean our air. They absorb CO2, they produce oxygen, they capture particulate matter. They capture stormwater. So they actually reduce flooding and reduce pressure on our aging stormwater systems. That's extremely important in climate change. Beyond climate, trees are incredibly good for mental health. There's a huge body of literature that says just the fact that we have access to green space, we feel less stress, we concentrate better, we have better mental health. For kids, they play, they learn, they explore. It's very healthy. Adults, if they walk under trees, their blood pressure goes down, they recover attention. Hospitals that have trees view recover faster. They need less painkillers. Trees are also incredibly good for community and local economies. They tend to increase property values. They increase foot traffic. Less crime. It's very healthy for commerce. It makes our streets more walkable. It makes us less car dependent. If we plant in lower income neighborhoods, which have less trees and more heat and more pollution, it's very important for equity. For environmental justice. So yes, trees are important. The only concern is that they require maintenance. They require water. Young trees die very easily if not properly maintained. We need to plant the right species in the right place. Otherwise, they can crack the sidewalks, they can block your views, they can increase allergies. We have to plan well. We have to diversify species. We have to engage the community. We have to budget for maintenance. Trees can sometimes be a pressure factor for gentrification, for green gentrification. People are afraid that if I plant trees, my property value will increase, my rents will increase, and I'll be displaced. And that can happen. Trees can hit power lines, they can hit infrastructure, pipes and so on. But I think it's a very healthy ecosystem. I think that if we plant them properly, if we take care of them, the benefits far outweigh the disadvantages. Cities without trees are very expensive. Much more expensive than the cost of maintenance. So they are like the skeleton of the city. They are the backbone. They clean our air, they cool our streets, they calm our minds, they connect our neighborhoods. They connect people. If we take care of them, if we invest in them, we will have a more healthy and resilient and equitable city. And we should do that.

text: I think about how does a yoga studio actually function. It's obviously just a room with mats, very quiet, calm. But there's so much more to it than just mats. It is a business, it is a community, it is a scheduling. So first of all, if you come into a yoga studio, you will first encounter the front desk. And the front desk has a very important role. First, to welcome people, to check in people. And some studios will ask for waivers to be signed before you do class, that type of thing. They will tell you where to put your shoes, where to put your bag, where to put your coat. Sometimes, for people that are new to yoga, they will give them a little orientation and say, hey, this is where the props are, this is how you set up your mat, and this is what to expect. And they will also sell class passes, they will sell memberships, they will sell reservations, they will collect payment. So a lot of studios, their front desk is really the social hub of their business. People come in and ask questions, people recognize each other. Second thing is scheduling. Most studios offer different types of classes, hatha yoga, vinyasa, yin, restorative, power, hot yoga, etc. And they usually label them with levels, so beginner, intermediate, advanced, etc. And they will schedule them accordingly. So we will see early morning classes for people that have work, mid-day classes for people that have more flexible schedule. We will see evening classes for people that come after work. We will see weekend workshops, teacher trainings, things like that. So a studio needs to figure out what classes are filling up and what classes are not, and then adjust their schedule accordingly. And also the capacity of the room, the availability of the teachers, the season, all of that matters. Third thing is teachers. Teachers are very important for the practice, of course. Teachers are not just leading you through a pose. Teachers are assessing the room, they are assessing the students, they are creating a sequence that is safe, that is dynamic, that will challenge people and also slow them down. They will give you alternatives, they will demonstrate alternatives. They will ask you if you're hurting, what you're feeling. And they will create a safe space, a calm space where you can concentrate and focus. They come early, they prepare the room, they come early, they set up the music, they set up the lights, they stay later to answer questions. Most teachers are freelancers, independent contractors, they are paid per class, or they are paid by headcount, or they are paid flat rate. And most of them will be teaching at several studios in order to fill their hours. Fourth thing is the business model. So studios will make money from drop-ins, they will make money from passes, they will make money from memberships, from workshops, from retail, from teacher trainings, things like that. Their expenses are rent, it's utilities, it's insurance, it's cleaning, it's props, booking system, marketing, paying teachers, etc. And because rent does not change whether you have an empty class or a full class, they really need to attract regular people, regular members, so they can have a very predictable income. And so that's why they will try to convert people from drop-ins to memberships. They will offer a first class or a first few classes for very cheap and then try to convert them into regulars. And some studios are for-profit, some are non-profit, some are co-ops, some are community spaces. And some will have a sliding scale or a pay what you can model, etc. Fifth thing is the space itself, the operations. So the floor has to be cleaned, the room has to be cleaned, the temperature and the humidity has to be managed. The props have to be cleaned, have to be replaced sometimes. The sound system, the lights, the mirrors, the ventilation, all of that is important. And then there's a lot of behind the scenes. So you have the booking system, the waitlist, the cancellation, the refund, the communication with students, the marketing, the social media, the email newsletter, the community events, things like that. And some studios, like a hot yoga studio, will really have to focus on the ventilation and heating. Other studios, that are very quiet and restorative, they will focus more on the lighting, etc. And then the last thing is community. So a yoga studio, when it's functioning well, is very much a community. People will be friends, teachers will know people's names, they will know their injuries, they will know their goals. They will host workshops, retreats, charity classes, meditation sessions. So it's really a space where you can relax and calm down and really feel welcome. And that will help with retention. People don't come to the studio just to do exercise, they come to feel community, to feel belonging. But at the same time, the studio has to keep a certain level of professionalism and boundaries in order to create an inclusive space that does not become cliquey, that is welcoming for everybody, that has safety and ethics. So that's a little bit about how a yoga studio works.

text:
I went to a used car dealership recently, there's this guy in a tube suit waving around, and then there's these rows and rows of cars. And I always think that's a very philosophical place actually. Cause it really represents life and time. All of these cars were somebody's. They were either over-grown or neglected or loved. And I was just standing there in the sun, this huge expanse of asphalt. And all these cars with their stickers, their prices written in marker. And I thought, what an incredible compression of life in that sticker, in that price.

And I was looking for a car because my car has been acting up. The check engine light has been on, and it just barely starts. It acts very weird when it's braking or stopping or turning. It just feels a bit unreliable. And I don't want to buy a new car. I want to buy a used car. But I want something that is reliable.

So I walked around this place. And there was a guy named Daryl who came out to greet me. He's a salesman, very nice guy. And he walked me through the lot. And he gave me some history on a lot of these cars. This one is owned by a school teacher who only drives to church and that's it. This one is owned by a retiree who has every single receipt. This one was owned by a teenager, so he probably treats it like it's a game. And I liked one car in particular. It was a little silver car, and it smelled like lemon and coffee. And it started very nicely. It only has 89,000 miles. And I thought, wow, that's a lot of miles, but that's also nice, that it has a past. That it has been somewhere. That it has been used.

So we took it for a spin on the highway. And it was okay. It pulled a little bit to the right, but I pretended that I didn't notice it. And we drove around. And he talked to me about all the warranties, financing, whatever. And I asked him, did it have any accidents? And he said no. And I thought, I don't know whether I believe him or not. I think that's what makes used car buying fun and scary. You're just gonna trust somebody.

And then we negotiated in his office. And I had my car there as a trade-in. And I actually saw it from his office, and it looked so sad. But it was my car, and it carried me through so many things. My moves, my heartbreaks, my trips. It was like a little album, my car. But I traded it in, and we negotiated, and I bought the car.

And I drove off the lot. And I saw this tube man behind me, waving, selling air to no one. And I thought, we're all used cars in life, right? We come with miles, we come with bumps and bruises and scratches. We come with things we don't really disclose about our life. And we hope that somebody will look at us and still see value in us. And this car that I bought, it's not perfect. It rattles a little bit. It has a stain in the backseat that looks like a tiny country. But it starts in the morning. And that's what's important. It's not shiny, it's not new, it's not perfect. But it will start and take me somewhere. So that's enough. And I drove away with my windows open. I just felt so nice and happy.

And then I kept thinking about this. And I really feel that sometimes compromise is not a bad thing. That compromise can be a beautiful thing, that it's a way of getting things done when you can't have perfection. And I'm very happy that I bought this car. And the key in my pocket is a little scratched and battered, but it works. So I feel very happy.

text:
Ms. Albright used to have a uniform, navy blue polyester that wouldn't hang right, would just stick out from your body. Really awful material. She hated that uniform. Used to get a rash around the collar because it was so stiff and starched. She's here in her classroom now, thirty years later. And this uniform is nicer, it's a softer cotton, it fits better, it's more comfortable. But it does the same thing. That sea of navy and white. It kind of erases a lot of who they are.

There's a boy in the back row who's new, Leo. And his uniform is too big, his blazer, the sleeves, he just has his hands in there. And he keeps pulling on the collar, tugging on the button. He's making this little cathedral out of paperclips. He's got it on his desk, in silent reading. Everyone's reading. He's just making this little cathedral or spaceship out of paperclips. She walks over. He looks up at her. He looks at her with this big eyes, like, uh oh. And she just kneels down. She says, "That is beautiful. What is it?" He just shrugs and says, "Just a thing." And she says, "It looks like a place where I would want to live. A place with no rules." And he smiles just a little bit. He looks at her suit, her grey suit, her very sensible shoes. He looks at the uniformity of her. And then he looks away.

Then at recess she watches him. He's over by the fence and he's not with the other kids. He's just drawing in the dirt with his toe. And they're all playing kickball. He's just drawing in the dirt. And the uniform makes him look very separate from them. It doesn't really include him, it just separates him from the rest of them. And it's a very sad thing. He's just looking very lost.

And then he leaves and she has a note on her desk that a little girl has written. A very shy girl. Chloe. Who hardly talks. And it says, "Leo's paperclip thing was cool." And she looks over at Chloe. Chloe is very neat. Her uniform is very neat, no wrinkles. She's very neat. And she's packing her bag and very quietly. But she looked at Leo's paperclip cathedral and thought it was cool. And she saw him.

And then they leave. And Ms. Albright stays in the classroom. And the room is very quiet. And she thinks about how she hated the uniform. And how it erases people. And it's her job to find who they are underneath the uniform. She walks over to the back and Leo left his little paperclip cathedral there. And he left it very carefully. And next to it he has a little button. A button from the uniform. He put it there very carefully, very deliberately. And Ms. Albright picks up the button. It's very smooth and it's very cool and it's white. And it's just a little uniform button. And she picks it up. And it's nothing. And it's so little. But it feels very special to her. And she holds it in her fist, in her hand.

text: I think going through the Alps in a train is one of the most special travel experiences you can do in life. But what happens? A line needs to get to higher altitude, and then to pass the mountain range. So it can't do a straight line, it needs to negotiate through the valley, the tunnels, the curves, the bridges. And then come down safely. It doesn't matter if it's the Glacier Express from St. Moritz to Zermatt, or the Bernina Express going to Italy, or the other line through Gotthard, the general logic is the same. So, it starts normally in a big city, Zurich, Milan, Munich, Vienna. Starts in the big station, goes through the suburbs, through the industry. Follows a river, follows a lake. Then it starts climbing, and slowly the landscape starts closing, the nature starts closing. Fields, then trees, then the mountain. A railway line doesn't like steep gradients, because the friction, adhesion, between the wheel and the rail is not very good. So it goes up very slowly. It goes up in the valley, and turns and turns and turns to gain height. It looks like it's going in a wrong direction, but actually, it's very calculated. And when it goes up, it passes stone viaducts, small tunnels, villages, and the tracks are very close to the village. And then the spiral tunnels, or loop tunnels, where you enter into the mountain, you turn around in the tunnel, and you exit higher. And then you're facing the same valley, but from a different angle. And then, for the steepest gradients, there is the rack railway, where there is a rail in the middle, with teeth, that engages with the train, and it can really go up very steep. But modern railways, they try to avoid that. They want to build huge tunnels through the mountain. Like Gotthard base tunnel, that is 57 km long. That's below the Alps, that goes through the mountain and completely avoids the climb. Then, the line is very complex, and very managed. Because it's always electrified, it's always signalled. It's very difficult to keep the signal and keep the rail working properly in snow, in fog, in rocks. It's very single track, so it needs to pass at stations or in loops. It needs to be scheduled very carefully. There are all these barriers to protect from avalanches, or from rocks falling, from snow. There are snow fences, there are heated switches. And in winter, the team comes and cleans the platforms, and checks the tracks. In summer, there's heat, thunderstorms, that can cause problems. Behind the scenes, there are guys that manage the traffic, because it goes across international borders, so it's very complex to manage. And then you travel in a very panoramic carriage, that has very large curved windows, that lets you see the landscape very easily. And the carriage floats over the landscape. And you see these terraced fields.

text: I had headphones that I got from my brother for my birthday. And these headphones are noise-cancelling and they cost $300. I was walking in the hospital with these headphones on. It was very noisy in the hallway and I really liked that silence. My dad is in the room 412. And he was awake. And he looked at me and he doesn't recognize me very well. And he said, what is this? And I said, noise-cancelling headphones. And he said, what? I said, noise-cancelling headphones. He said, for noise? Yeah. How? I explained to him, I showed him the headphones. There are microphones. It listens to the room, to the noise in the room. And then it samples it thousands of times per second and it takes that sound wave and turns it upside down. It creates a mirror image of the wave. And then it plays that mirror image. So when the two waves meet, they cancel each other out. He said, so it meets itself and disappears? Yeah. And he said, you create silence with noise. And I said, it's either very smart or very sad. And he was very quiet and I said, both, and I laughed. And he said, when your mom died, I would wake up at night and listen to the house and the refrigerator, the clock, the wind outside. And I would listen to everything to not feel the silence. And I said, and it worked? No. And I didn't say anything. I was just listening. I used to do the same thing with him. I was listening to his coughs, his breathing, his sounds, his voice, to feel him. text: I think remote work is very good in terms of flexibility, no commute, no shared spaces with other people, and no distraction. And yet, for some people, especially, it can cause loneliness. And loneliness is very, very complicated. Being alone is not the same as loneliness. Loneliness is having a gap between the social connection that you want and the social connection that you actually get. So remote work can amplify that and very easy to get lonely. The problem is that we are very social people and loneliness, chronic loneliness, is associated with many diseases, from depression and anxiety to cardiovascular problems, sleep problems, cognitive decline. So remote work, why does it cause loneliness? First of all, remote work eliminates ambient sociality. In a regular office, a lot of social interaction is very incidental. You talk with somebody in the coffee room. You talk with somebody while going to a meeting. You overhear a joke or you ask a question. Those little things are very important because they create weak ties that make you feel part of something and they are so easy. And in remote work, everything is very intentional. You have to call somebody or you have to message or have a meeting and a meeting needs an agenda. So it's very easy to go days without very casual interactions. And that can feel very lonely, even if you have your calendar full. Second, remote work makes interactions very narrow. On video call, you only see words and some facial expression. And sometimes, those things are very performative or transactional. You don't have peripheral awareness, you don't have side conversations, you don't have people coming over to your desk, you don't have shared spaces. So it's very easy to feel that you're doing something very transactional, very status oriented, very task oriented and not relationship oriented. Zoom fatigue, people complain about that a lot. And then you have text chat that is very efficient but it can be very ambiguous, very hard to read the tone. So sometimes people feel that they're not really able to get to know each other. And they end up feeling more and more lonely, even though they talk to people all day, because those interactions don't satisfy. Sometimes, it even backfires and people become introverted. Third, remote work removes boundaries, so it removes time for social interaction. People start earlier, people work later. They answer messages at night. Their home becomes their office. And their office doesn't really end. So it's very easy to feel too exhausted to meet somebody, to go to a club, to see somebody. At the same time, you don't have the social support of colleagues that you had before. You can complain to them, you can celebrate things with them. So the effects are doubled. Not only you have more stress that comes from working, but also you don't have someone to process that stress with. And then, remote work impacts people in a very asymmetric way. Some people are in the industry for a very long time and they have a very strong network. They have a partner, they have a very active social life. They can thrive in remote work. Some other people, early career people, new hires, people that came to another country, they live alone, they are more extroverted, they have less social networks, they will suffer a lot more. New hires miss out a lot on mentorship and on informal learning that happens in offices. People that live alone may go a whole day without talking to someone in person. Or people that are parents, they feel lonely in a different way. They are surrounded by people but they don't have peers. So it's very context dependent. And remote work can also help, for example, people that are introverted, people that have some disability, people that feel discriminated against in office. So remote work is a life saver for them. Now, the very good news is that loneliness is not a given in remote work. And you can improve it a lot. And this is something that companies should really design. They should create opportunities for very casual interactions. Virtual coffees, no agenda. Mentorship programs, employee resource groups, one on ones that really address well-being, not just performance. Some occasional in-person meetups. And managers should really model the boundaries, not send messages at night, have space for non-work interactions. Hybrid is also very good because it preserves some in-person interactions. It doesn't mean that people will be friends, but it creates social infrastructure. For individuals, what can they do? They can schedule social interaction as they schedule meetings. They can go to coworking spaces, clubs, classes, etc. They can create rituals. I do walks with a neighbor, I have lunch with my friends. I have a game night every week online, and so on. They can define a very clear end to workday. They can have a very specific space at home for work. Some people, therapy and groups can really help, especially when loneliness becomes chronic and is associated with anxiety or depression. And we have to really accept that loneliness is a signal, not a judgement. In conclusion, remote work and loneliness are connected because it removes the incidental, the embodied, the very structured social interactions that we had before. And it makes interactions very intentional, very narrow and easy to postpone. And the risk is higher for people that have less social networks outside of work, for early career people. But remote work is not the enemy. We have to design it better, we have to have boundaries, we have to have rituals, we have to have mentorship and some in-person. text:
I really hate the notion that an audio guide is a neutral thing. So often people just take them, they click on it, they walk through the museum, but they're completely distracted from the work. I've had great experiences with audio guides where it really opens up the painting, opens up the sculpture, tells you all the history, all the anecdotes, all the things that you'd never know otherwise. But at the same time, I've also been to museums where I'm just looking at the screen of the audio guide, or the little number on the wall, that's not really a neutral thing. So I think it's very valuable as a tool, but as long as it's optional, as long as it's very well-designed, and it's very selective. But the moment that it takes away from that very physical experience of looking at an artwork, thinking, feeling, it's kind of an issue.

The main advantage of audio guides is that it really brings people into these artworks. A lot of artworks are quite obscure, they don't tell you what they mean. So audio guides can really explain iconography, context, materiality, provenance, controversies, all of these things. And they can translate that very specialist vocabulary into very accessible language. So it's very valuable. Especially for blind or low-vision people. You can get audio description tours. So they can experience visual art too. It's also very valuable for people who speak a different language. And for kids, for casual visitors, it can really make it into a story. It can give it characters, conflicts, discoveries, all of these things. And then, you can go at your own pace. You can replay it, pause it, skip it. So it's very valuable and very democratizing. But at the same time, this voice that you're listening to, it becomes a very strong authority. It tells you what to look at, what to see, what to pay attention to. And it assigns a very specific meaning to a painting that maybe would've been very moving or puzzling on its own. So you just kind of go through the museum like checking boxes. You look at one artwork, you hear the number, then you move on. You are very isolated with your headphones. You don't talk to the person next to you. And you don't discover things together. And then, a lot of times, the audio guides are very long, very detailed. You really get cognitively overloaded. You're listening more than you're looking. And it can be very annoying, especially with a technical glitch, with a bad interface, or with people around you. And not every work needs an audio guide. I think there's a lot of value in silence and in ambiguity and in slow looking. But, yeah, I think that if it's done very well, if it's optional, if it's very concise, very selective, and it's layered, so you can get a very brief orientation that invites questions rather than answers. That's very valuable. And then it can also be very direct. Instead of saying, this painting is about despair or about war, it says, look at the brushwork on the left, look at this detail. And then, you can also have multiple voices. So it's not only the curator, but maybe the artist, maybe a community member, maybe a critic. And you can take it as a scaffold, and then you can just listen for five minutes, then take it out, look at the painting. And that's kind of ideal. But I wouldn't say that it's a bad thing, just that it can go very wrong. I think that audio guides really help and open doors and make things more accessible. But I just don't want it to become a corridor, something that takes you from A to B and very prescribed. And I think that the ideal is that there's a rhythm of listening and looking, guidance and freedom. And if it helps you see better, then it works. If it prevents you from seeing, just turn it off.

And they gave me until Sunday to come take what I want. But it's not in the house, it's outside. It's the smell of the dirt and the tomato leaves and the lavender that grows just in a crooked line. When I was nine, after my parents split up, she taught me how to garden. And she just knelt down next to me and she said, "You don't yank, you just ask the dirt. You ask it gently for what you need." But last week I went to see her and she just looked out the window and she said, "The tomatoes need staking." And I said, "Yes, they do." "Use the twine in the shed, the brown one, not the green." And I said, "Yes, I will." And she just nodded and then she closed her eyes and I just felt she was gone. And so I came and I put the groceries on the porch and I walked in. The door was creaky. And the little stone walkway that she built, just putting one stone on top of the other, you can barely see it because of the thyme that grows over it. And I just got down and I pulled a little weed and the dirt is just so nice and loose and just full of worms. And then Mrs. Alvarez from next door, she was working in her yard, and she said, "You're gonna get dirty." And I said, "I don't mind." And she said, "She's gonna be happy that someone is taking care of it." And she said, "She used to say the garden is a conversation. If you don't talk to it, it forgets about you." And I laughed, but I just coughed. I said, "She forgets a lot of things these days." And she said, "Not this. She asks me every time I come, 'How's the garden doing? Are the figs ripe?'" And by late afternoon, it looked much better. It wasn't fixed, but it just looked much better. And the sun was going down and I just sat on the bench by the birdbath and I watched the bees just stumble into the foxglove and it was just very golden and beautiful. And then my phone rang. And it was the memory care unit. And I answered and I said, "Hi." And the nurse said, "Your grandmother is asking for you. She wants to talk about the garden." So I drove there. And I got there and I said, "I'm here." And she just grabbed my hand. And her hands were very cold, but she was very strong, holding on. And she said, "The tomatoes." And I said, "Yes, I put them up. I put the brown twine." And she just smiled and she said, "Good girl." And she said, "And the figs?" And I said, "Not yet." And she said, "They'll come. You have to wait." And we just sat there and watched the sun going down. And the parking lot was just gray and nothing. And I just looked out the window and I just felt the garden. And I just squeezed her hand and she squeezed back. And then she closed her eyes and I just stayed there until the nurse came and said that she needs to go. And then I drove home. And I just stood in the garden and listened to the crickets and the garden was very quiet. But it was there.

text:
I was just cleaning out my hallway the other day, dusting the bookshelves and I pulled down a book that my grandmother had given me a long time ago. Very old book. The cover is actually completely faded and discolored and the dust jacket is not there anymore. And as I was opening it, I actually found a photo that was tucked between the pages. Just fell out. This very small square photo with the little scalloped edges. And I turned it over and there was no writing on it, no date, no name, nothing. Just this chemical smell that old photos have. And I just turned it over.

And I was shocked because this photo is black and white but it's so bright. It's very sunny. And it's my grandmother. She's under a tree and she's laughing, very happy, laughing with her head thrown back. And she's holding her hat. And there's a young man next to her with the shirt rolled up that is looking at her. Not looking at the camera, just looking at her. And it took me a second to actually recognize her. Because I only know her in her old age. And in her very old age. And I really had a hard time recognizing that this could be her. She's very young, like 19. And this person is so beautiful and radiant and happy. And I didn't know her.

I just sat down on the floor. And I was reading this book that I read in college and I actually had written in it. And it was very funny how this photo was in the book and I had just moved it from one apartment to the next and I hadn't even opened the book. And it's very strange to me that it was in this particular book that was about love and time and longing. And it's very nice that I found it. And that it was tucked away in the book. I don't think it was just by chance. I think that it was just waiting to be found. And maybe it's just one of the things that books do, they keep things. Not just words. They keep things.

So I looked at it and I really enjoyed looking at it and trying to recognize all the details. And the tree that is behind her is an elm and it's very green and lush. And her hat is a straw hat. And she's wearing a sleeveless dress, very light. And the young man is smiling very gently and very nice. And I really wondered, who took the photo, and what happened after the photo was taken. Did they go to the lake? Did they argue? Did they get married? Did they even know that it was so beautiful and that it would turn into a memory? And my grandmother never told me about that day. Maybe she forgot about it. Or maybe she just didn't want to keep that memory. I don't know. But it's very nice.

So I left the photo on my desk now. And it's still there and it's leaning against this pen holder and I look at it and I feel this very tender feeling. Not quite sadness, but almost. But the fact that, every person that I've loved that's older, I really didn't meet the young version of them. That's really what it is. And then I looked out of the window. And I just really enjoyed this afternoon. And that very ordinary afternoon will turn into a photo that maybe somebody will find in a book someday. And the book now is empty. But I think it's better that the photo is just there on the table. And that it's in the light and not hidden in the book. Because sometimes we just have to find those things. And it's very, very nice.

text: I bought a property. When I first opened the door, I was so disappointed that I stood and didn't enter. But I did move in, knowing that I would be renovating this place. Because I was so disappointed, or maybe just tired, I didn't know what I wanted to see the construction go exactly, or all the tiling and painting and floors. I just got sick of having rooms that are very small and cramped and dark. I didn't really want to look into the details of what would the kitchen look like or what color would the walls be. I just wanted something light, light and light. That's it. It's very simple. And then the construction started. It is always very noisy, so loud. And the walls come down. And when you come down the walls, you see the old walls. There were different wallpapers and layers and layers of people who lived there before. And it is very nice to see that. It is very emotional. So I think that renovation is very nice. But also I was living in this house during the construction, and it was very challenging. I just ate dinner every day in the box on a chair. And everything was plastic covered. And then after I went to bed at night, everything was covered with dust. Dust everywhere. Dust in my hair, in my books, in my phone. I just used to say, this is the past that I am sanding away. This is the past that is making this dust that I am seeing. So it was very very emotional. And I think it is also kind of romantic to see all the dust that comes from the different walls and different ceilings that you are sanding and demolishing. But at the same time it's very challenging. Because you need to just keep going, keep demolishing, keep sanding. But it never looks good until the very last, like 80% of the renovation is done. And at some point, the renovation looks beautiful, and then it goes down again. Like that two weeks before I moved in, it looked horrible. I was just like, this is terrible, I don't want to move in here. And then the very last weekend, it looked perfect, so I moved in. But during that process, it's very challenging to see the results that come with the designs. The tiles that you select and the color of the walls and everything. You don't see it for a very long time. There are delays, there are problems. So you have to really, really just commit to what you want and keep going. And then there are a lot of decisions that are small, but they are very big. Choosing a very small detail of the grout or the tiles or the walls. Which color I want, which white I want. Which gray I want. So these decisions feel very important and very difficult. And then I did it. And now I very much love what I have. Very simple design. I have light oak floor. I love it very much. I also love the color of my kitchen cabinet. It's a green. And I love my white tiles in the bathroom, very simple. And now I very much love what I see. I think it is very nice. And when I open the door, I very much love this house. It doesn't make me disappointed anymore. And I think the renovation changed my life in the sense that I pay attention to different things. And I like the house very much. And this is exactly what I wanted. I think that before I was very skeptical about it. And I now very much like having the house that I know from inside, that I know how I used the space, that I like it, that I really wanted to design it. And I think this is very nice. So I'm very happy with the result. And what I want to keep in mind is that it's not finished. I think it's important to remember that renovation is never finished. It's never perfect. So I want to always remember that things will scratch, things will stain. Things will age. And that's ok. This is how life is. I don't want to make my home perfect and clean and museumy. I want it to live. I want to age it. I want it to be my own. And I want the scratches. I want the stains. I want the use and the life that will come. That's what I want. And that's what I have. And I think in the future I will scratch the floor. And I already scratched it very lightly. And it was very nice to see because it means I really live here. And I very much like this.

text:
We often hear very negative thoughts around price increases for any product. The consumer feels betrayed. The consumer thinks, the same product, same brand, why is it more expensive? The price increase is not always a bad thing, but I think what is bad is when it is not justified, it is not transparent, and the value is not being provided. So a price increase is justified when the supplier or the manufacturer faces a real cost increase. Things are becoming more expensive, raw materials, energy, transport, labor, compliance. If you don't pass it through, you might have to reduce the quality of the product, or reduce the staff, or reduce maintenance, or you might go bankrupt. Which is not very convenient for the customer either. So sometimes, a small price increase is better than the quality of the product falling. And then, the customer says, okay, I'm paying more than before, but I get the same product or the same service that I always got. It's a very human thing, that the consumer is always looking for the minimum price. But if we make the most affordable product, in general, the quality is going to suffer. So we need to find a balance.

But then, of course, the consumer feels very badly when it's a very modest income. So the same price increase is not perceived in the same way. So it's very important to do it in a transparent way. And to explain to the customer why we are doing it. For example, we need to pay more for raw material or we need to pay more for transport or energy. So the customer can understand it. And sometimes the consumer feels very betrayed, when the price goes up, but the quality goes down. And that's very common. That's very difficult. So it's very important that the company does it in a transparent way, and it needs to communicate to the customer. The customer can always change product or brand, of course, that's true. The company knows that. So it's very important that the company does not do the price increase in a very tricky way. Like reducing the size of the product and saying, "I haven't increased the price." That's very tricky. And it's very bad. Or if the company can give loyalty discounts, bulk discounts, or give cheaper options to the customer. That's very good. So the customer can decide to buy the same quantity, but it's more expensive. Or buy a bit less, but the same quality.

And the other thing is that if there are many competitors, the customer can switch. So the company, in a competitive market, cannot increase the price a lot, otherwise it will lose customers. In very non-competitive markets, the customer is very captive. So in that case, the price increase is more difficult for the customer, and maybe some regulation is needed. Or scrutiny from the public, to see whether the price increase is justified. So a price increase is never a betrayal, I think. But it should be very well explained and justified and transparent. And the value has to be given to the customer. That's very important. If the price goes up and the value is given, the customer is happy. So it's very important that the consumer also claims their rights, asks questions and compares prices and demands the value. That's very important.
